name: Potassium permanganate soaks

card.summary: A very dilute purple potassium permanganate bath or soak, traditionally used as an astringent antiseptic for weepy, blistering or infected skin, helping skin look calmer and drier.
card.note: Concentrated forms burn skin, stain, and are toxic if swallowed; no FDA-approved medical use.

quick.overview:
Potassium permanganate is a strong oxidising salt that turns water deep purple. In a very dilute soak it acts as an antiseptic and astringent, and doctors have long used it for skin that is weeping, crusted or infected, as in some eczema flares, impetigo or fungal foot infections.

The appearance payoff is calmer, drier, less inflamed skin during those flares. It is no longer the preferred treatment: Wikipedia notes that it is no longer first-line in dermatology, and newer antiseptics replaced it in wound guidelines.
quick.how: In dermatology, a dilute solution was applied as a bath, a foot soak or a soaked dressing for a short period, with petroleum jelly sometimes used on nails to limit staining. UK guidance such as the Drug and Therapeutics Bulletin has addressed how to reduce harm from soaks. Specific dilutions should come from a prescriber or product label.
quick.risks: Undiluted crystals or strong solutions can cause chemical burns, and an undissolved tablet has caused a severe burn in a child. Solutions can stain skin, nails and clothing, irritate skin, and are toxic if swallowed. The FDA reports no approved medical use in the US. Vaginal insertion used as misuse has caused serious injury.

lead: Potassium permanganate soaks use a very dilute aqueous solution of potassium permanganate, a purple oxidising compound, as a bath, foot soak or compress. [1][2] It has been used as an astringent and antiseptic for fluid-producing skin conditions, including eczema, impetigo, fungal foot infections and superficial wounds, with the goal of drying and cleansing the skin so it looks calmer. [1]

Potassium permanganate was first synthesised in the 1600s and was in common medical use by at least the 1800s; Henry Bollmann Condy marketed disinfectant solutions later known as 'Condy's crystals'. [1] The Grokipedia entry dates its first synthesis to 1659 by Johann Rudolf Glauber. [2]

Today it is not the preferred treatment. Wikipedia reports that it is no longer favoured in dermatology and has been made obsolete by newer antiseptics and antifungals, and a 2021 review of wound antiseptics lists it among older agents that guidelines no longer recommend for wounds. [1][3] A 2023 Drug and Therapeutics Bulletin article addresses minimising harm from soaks. [4]

angle.text: A dilute soak was used to dry and disinfect blistering, weeping or infected skin, which helps the skin look and feel less inflamed. It is a medical-style treatment for particular conditions, not a general cosmetic.

infobox: No FDA-approved medical use; Rx tablets in US; on WHO Essential Medicines list [1]

paras: Traditional dermatological uses include fungal foot infections, impetigo, pemphigus, superficial wounds, dermatitis and topical ulcers, typically conditions that produce a lot of fluid; it was applied as a soaked dressing or bath. [1] For eczema, it was recommended only for a few days at a time because it irritates skin. [1] A 1964 Practitioner article on eczema is among the historical references. [5]

A review of skin cleansing in children notes that antiseptics such as potassium permanganate or chlorhexidine can be added to bath water for impetiginised dermatoses. [6] It has also been used historically to wash out the stomach in certain poisonings, and it is widely used in water treatment. [1][2]

Wikipedia reports that effective bactericidal action needs about 1:5,000 or stronger, which is irritating, so 1:10,000 solutions were usually used, and some bacteria survived even that. [1] The British National Formulary in 2015 described dissolving 100 mg in a litre of water for a 0.01% solution. [1] Manganese dioxide forms on contact and stains skin. [1]

Topical use can cause skin irritation and discolouration of skin and clothing, and higher concentrations can cause chemical burns; an undissolved tablet caused a severe burn in a child. [1] It is toxic if swallowed. Concentrated solutions have caused airway swelling and respiratory distress, and roughly 10 grams may be fatal. [1]

Other documented misuse includes insertion into the vagina to induce abortion, which the FDA reports is ineffective and causes serious injury, and rectal exposure has been reported as a cause of chemical colitis. [1][7] Reviews note the vagina can absorb potassium permanganate. [8]

In the US, potassium permanganate has no FDA-approved medical uses, tablets are sold by prescription, and the FDA does not recommend the crystal or tablet form except as a diluted liquid; it appears on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines. [1]

Evidence is mostly historical and clinical-guideline in nature. A 2021 review of wound antiseptics lists potassium permanganate among older antiseptics not recommended for wound treatment in current Polish and German guidance. [3] A registered trial, NCT00610324 (n=512, completed), compared oral decontamination with chlorhexidine or potassium permanganate in ICU patients for pneumonia, and trial NCT02546804 (n=90) compared two homemade mouthwashes in gum disease; their results are not summarised here. [9][10]
